title: Semantic models in the Power BI service

claims.text: A semantic model is a data source prepared for reporting and visualization; apart from streaming models, every semantic model is a data model built on Analysis Services tabular modeling technology.

Semantic models can originate several ways: publishing a Power BI Desktop model, uploading an Excel workbook or CSV file, connecting to an externally hosted Analysis Services model, or creating push and streaming models through the service APIs.
Power BI Desktop supports three model storage modes - Import, DirectQuery, and Composite - distinguished by whether the data is copied into the model or left in the underlying source at query time.
An Import-mode model hosted in the Power BI service must be loaded entirely into memory before it can answer queries.

Import-mode models serve a snapshot of data and rely on scheduled or on-demand refresh to stay current, whereas DirectQuery models forward queries to the source so results always reflect current source data.
Both Import and DirectQuery models need an on-premises data gateway whenever their source data is not reachable directly over the internet.

Reports can live-connect to models hosted outside Power BI in SQL Server Analysis Services or Azure Analysis Services; SSAS requires an on-premises data gateway while Azure Analysis Services connects without one, and the report user's identity is used to enforce data permissions.

Reusing an existing enterprise Analysis Services model through a live connection is a recommended approach when an organization already has data-warehouse model investments, instead of rebuilding the model inside Power BI.
Row-level security roles in a semantic model are either dynamic, filtering data based on the identity of the report user, or static, applying one fixed filter to every user assigned to the role.

Changing a semantic model's gateway and cloud connection settings requires ownership of the model; non-owners see it read-only, and ownership can be taken over programmatically (for example when the original owner leaves the organization).

The main levers that determine a semantic model's impact on capacity resources are where the model is hosted, its storage mode, gateway dependencies, the volume of imported data, and the type and frequency of refresh.
